Having played this games series to completion (well, almost: what, you mean to tell me that you actually got all the way through  Postal 3?!), I feel that reviewing them all is necessary. This game, however, is going to be difficult to review. It's not that it's a badly made game or that I hate it (on the contrary). The problem is that it's such a disturbing game that I may end up on a watchlist for recommending it. Whatever! Here it goes.

The first installment of the Postal series is of humble origins, provided that your definition of "humble origins" involves being banned in 14 countries, being blacklisted by most major retailers and being mentioned by Senator Joe Lieberman to the Senate as one of the "three worst things in American society" (the other two being Marilyn Manson and Calvin Klein underwear ads). Postal is a game about a guy (the Postal Dude) being bombarded with demonic mental images and voices convincing him to murder society as a whole. Each level is a neighborhood, truckstop, air force base, shopping mart, etc. of innocent people and hostile people ("hostile" being cops, government agents, well-armed vigilantes and other people who are merely trying to stop a madman with weapons from murdering everybody). You are instructed to kill at least 80-90% of the hostile people before progressing to the next level. Unlike the succeeding two games, the only morality choice you're really given is whether you want to kill only the people trying to kill you or kill everybody. 
The gameplay is a third person isometric, much like the first couple Army Men games that 3DO had, only with much more gore, suffering and people pleading for their lives. The weapons in this game are strictly military grade, unlike the succeeding two, and you don't have animals to help you, like the feral cats or your dog, Champ (although his doghouse is in the first level). 
Now, let's talk about the content. At the beginning of each level, you are treated with disturbing artwork of screaming people, corpses and evil humanoid entities with the soundtrack of "Texas Chainsaw Massacre" kinds of experimental percussion raging in the background. At the bottom of each of these loading screens is a diary entry of the Postal Dude, which usually reads like "The city is a refuse pile, and I come to exterminate the bugs. Clean the wound with more blood!" Afterwards, you start the level, where you murder people. While you can definitely perform much more sadistic and demented acts of cruelty in the sequels, they give it to you in a very zany, silly and whimsical manner. Whereas, with the first game, you're told to shoot and kill everything in a very serious manner. While the Postal Dude does give an occasional quip, there's very little hilarity in the game. Also like Texas Chainsaw Massacre, the game is a very demented piece of work, that although goes far out of its way to make you uncomfortable, is strangely appealing. 
  Anyway, the game is entertaining and worth a playthrough in my opinion, but be very careful as to who you play the game in front of.

The good ol' days, cleaning the attic and wonder at the relics you collected in your lifetime... so many beautiful memories with the people you cared the most, until you find a box titled ''old videogames'' and remember the money you wasted to entertain yourself, you opened the box, amongst the pile there is a certain one you pull out and blow the dust off, ''Postal'' is written in big words and decided to give it a try since you have little memory from it.
After hours of gaming, you realise why you buried your beloved ones in the backyard...

[h1] Story: [/h1]

You wear the boots of Postal dude, a man who believes that judgement day arrived, as you are preparing for such events the police comes knocking on your door with pistols and shotguns, you realise that everybody has gone insane, murder is the key to release their souls, you pick up your gun and make the skies rain crimson...

[h1] Gameplay: [/h1]

The controls in this game is simple besides the numpad, for weapon switching, which at some point you'll forget the number at said weapon and blow up or just burn yourself.

The game itself is based around the isometric perspective while some have a top-down view, its design sure is beautiful by how heavy the theme of the game is, the devs sure did a good job with the dark tones and the depressing ambience.

Main objective is to reach a certain percentage of murdered hostiles of each level, not only there is hostiles but inocents are present in the levels, of course if you want, you can add them to your killing list and with the addition of a ability to execute both hostile and inocents, if they survive being gunned down multiple times and trying to crawl away from you, the goal here is surviving massive waves of enemies with as much as your bloodthirst filled.

The achievements are at a medium level to achieve, some will take some time while one you'll just need painkillers and that's the ''Boondock's Saint'' which is to complete the campaign with zero inocents casualities, it sounds easy but most of the time they will get infront of the enemy's line and get shot by them, even if they get hit once, you will not get the achievement, good luck getting it...

Not to forget that the game has got a multiplayer mode for 15 players that can be used by LAN or the RWS servers, but due to some connection problems and glitches as well the servers had to be shut down sadly, the three modes is Going Postal, Capture The Flag and The March.

[h1] Glitches/bugs/erros report: [/h1]

To be honest, i didn't found that many glitches as i was hoping except when the enemies gets stuck in some corners and starts spinning and the game crashes after you restart the level too many times.

[h1] Overall: [/h1]

The game truly is a masterpiece in terms of how brutally dark it is, fun to play indeed, of course you'll sometimes get annoyed by the enemies and the inocents as well, some of the achievements can be a bit bugged and you'll just achieve them by playing the game after you quitting but i do recommend this game for anyone who likes this sort of theme or isn't afraid to adventure themselves with this jewel.

Score: 8/10

Postal 2 is one of the craziest games ever made, but it's time to take a look a the franchises humble beginnings. 

Story:

Postal is very light on story, but the basic gist is that you play as the Postal Dude who one day has had enough, so he picks up a gun and goes on a rampage killing every single person he sees. 

There's basically no story, each level is connected by a piece of writing at the start of the level and those have some insanely edgy writing to the point where it screams to the player saying "Hey look at me and how edgy I am". I don't really like these info dumps, I highly prefer Postal 2 and how that game does it's edgy story, with some humor instead of just pure edge. 

Graphics:

Postal is not the best looking game and has not aged gracefully in this department. So let's first start of with the good. The environments all look great and each level has it's own very distinct look and it's easy to tell where you are. However that's basically all good about the graphics.

The games main goal of hunting down people and killing them is easy to understand, but sometimes the NPC characters blend into the environments or sometimes walk somewhere where you simply can't see them and even though you don't need to kill them all to get a 100% sometimes becomes difficult because of this. Not to mention hope you enjoy killing the same four different type of people over and over until the game is over. 

Audio:

Postal is the best in the audio department. The Music is absolutely dreadful in my opinion, it's loud droning noises that will make your ears bleed. It's definitely edgy, but it sounds like absolute ass. Also most guns you use sounds like toys and hearing the same machine gun shooting over and over and people screaming constantly could drive someone insane. 

Gamplay:

Alright now about the gameplay. When most people think of Postal, they think about going around town and doing mundane tasks until crazy stuff happens. Here the only goal is to kill, kill, kill. You load into a map and you need to kill a certain amount of people to go to the next location and do this over and over until you're done. 

I'll admit the game is really fun, going around and mowing down people is pretty entertaining for a while, but a few of the design choices make the game get tedious pretty fast. First of all, most enemies take a ton of bullets to put down, it feels like you're shooting a terminator instead of a human. It Roughly takes over 40 bullets to take down, most of the enemies in the games which becomes tedious when you start fighting them in groups. 

There are easier ways to dispatch of them like fire and explosives, but the ammo for these is insanely limited, which makes you go back to the machine gun. I also stated before how enemies will end up wandering off and it's going to be a pain to try and track them down. 

Verdict:

Postal has not aged gracefully, there's a ton of issues that make this game more tedious than fun and I definitely prefer the second Postal game. However there's still some enjoyment to try out the game and see how different the game is to it's bonkers sequel. Since it's free the only thing you will lose is your time trying it out, but however if you really need to play this, then just play the remake instead.

Final Rating:
6/10

It is so astounding how good Postal is, especially when you consider the limitations the developers were likely working with back in 1997. Despite the age, the game succeeds in creating an uncomfortable atmosphere that many modern titles would struggle to replicate.

What impressed me the most is that the game represents much more than the violence you commit. That contrast makes the violence feel disturbing and uncomfortable, especially given how well the unsettling soundtrack fits with the gameplay. 

Even almost three decades after it's release, Postal remains effective because it understands what truly is scarier than any kind of gore. It is watching someone decend into pure madness and go postal. After all what is scarier, getting mauled by an eldritch horror, or slowly watching someone decend into madness and ruining their life in the process? The game becomes a disturbing psychological nightmare that stays with you for a while after playing it.

It is also very ironic that the developers considered a school shooting too grotesque to depict. Yet in hindsight that decision feels almost tragically accurate, as an unrelated real world tragedy would take place only a couple years later, and make such violence a horrifying reality.

This game is most certainly a classic, sparking the Postal age.

The thing about satire is that it’s not always comedic or farcical. The POSTAL franchise is known for its nihilistic comedy, but the original shares very little in common with its well-known sequel and other iterations.

1997’s POSTAL is a dark, arcade-like, top-over shooter that doesn’t shy from shocking imagery the draws parallels to the gun-violence epidemic in the United States. Art design harkens to Marilyn Manson and 1980s animated suburbia, marred with the shocking realism of blood-soaked and charred corpses. Levels have no progression and feel particularly random. They didn't know it then, but back in 1997 the developer Running with Scissors created a game that would become not only a landmark PC title, but one of the most controversial video games of all time. Little did they know the act of violence known as the Columbine Massacre committed two years later would be endlessly tied to both the POSTAL and Doom game series'.

The antagonist of the game is a schizophrenic man, known iconically as The Postal Dude, who has been evicted from his home. Being a conspiracy theorist, he believes that the United States Air Force has been releasing a mind-altering substance within the town of Paradise that has affected everyone but himself. Of course, the only way to solve this problem is to slaughter all of the humanoids and cleanse the earth of their infected presence. This more elaborate plot is not conveyed well within the game itself, despite the short dialogue in the loading screens that appear each time prior to progressing to the next level, rather it relied on the box art and manuals from back in the day to fully understand.

I won't spoil the ending for you, though I will say that it's not just the amount of killing that garnered this game such controversial fame; rather the very morbid subject matter, and dark humor-filled quips from the antagonist himself as he shows no mercy or remorse for his actions. This is a game that, while the plot is kept deliberately vague, taking the story and mental state of the main character into consideration makes it all the more disturbing and gruesome.

There are a total of 21 levels in POSTAL, most of which can be completed in just a few minutes each; the longevity of this title is not its strong point, clocking in at 1-2 hours for a full playthrough at best. Beginning at his home, The Postal Dude works his way through a truck stop, parade, trailer park, all the way to the military air base. This version does include the extra content from the Special Delivery expansion pack, which includes four new levels and the Gauntlet Challenge; the latter being a survival mode. Beware, however, as all of the co-op modes that were featured in the original release of this title are not available in this version; this is a single-player experience only.

The visuals within the game haven't aged incredibly well, but they're nothing to scoff at either. The backgrounds in particular are noteworthy, as they're completely hand-painted. The buildings and environments are wonderfully dark and morose, making way for an incredibly evil experience as The Postal Dude spills gallons of blood onto the ground. The character models are really what have aged terribly, as they're mini-verisons of models that would be found in games such as the original Resident Evil title for Playstation 1, and there aren't many different ones either. As far as a soundtrack goes, there's not one to speak of other than a looping set of guitar chords during the credits, although there are some subtle ambiances to be enjoyed; POSTAL is a game that plays better if you throw on your own "Mix to Kill By".

What will probably feel the most aged for modern gamers are the controls, this title no longer functions like any top-down isometric shooter of the current era. While you can set the game up to utilize your mouse, the mouse control becomes inverted at random intervals and becomes more frustrating than anything. It's best to stick to using the keyboard, where WSAD is used to move and the arrow keys are used to shoot. There's a decent guide in the forums for what's the best control set-up, so fear not if you need help.

With all of that being said, the original POSTAL still stands as a landmark game almost a decade later. For any fans of over-the-top, pointless violence, this is the game for you. The Postal Dude, despite not having a name and only having a small set of sarcastic, witty quotes, has become one of the most iconic characters in cult-classic fandom. Except for a few achievements, the game doesn't have much replayability or longevity, which is its only true downfall. However, at the price of $2.19 CAD, that's not extremely devastating. Still a classic, still dark, still blood-soaked, still fun, still worth buying. Long live The Postal Dude!

While Postal 2 was the high point of the series, without Postal there would be no Postal 2.

Postal is a game where you take control of The Postal Dude, a guy who's absolutely had it and finally decides GO POSTAL when he is evicted from his microscopic snowman home. The only people he needs to kill are the policemen that show up at his house before he even decides to shoot anyone, but it's much more fun to kill everybody, burning the people who try to escape from their homes. Every level starts out with a diary entry describing the day from the tortured perspective of the dude, complete with some spooky art that has become sort of a trademark to this game.

The game plays out very simple, you run around the maps looking for hostiles, which you can then exterminate with your large arsenal. Occasionally, there are secret areas with more hostilles and a special weapon, usually found on the edge of the map, but they aren't very common. The Postal dude can pick up healthkits, kevlar, backpacks, and stockpiles, which increase his health, armor, ammunition space, and ammo, respectively.

Enemies include policemen dressed in tan, which have the least amount of health and attack with pistols and shotguns, swat members dressed in blue, who attack with machineguns and shotguns, grenaders, who attack with their infinite supply of grenades and molotovs and have more health than the police, missile launchers, who shoot missiles at The Dude, which he can duck under, and turrets, which shoot missiles and bullets at you, and are easily killed with explosives.

For the weapons, you start with some kind of machinegun, which I believe is the only weapon that you can run and fire with at the same time, while also having infinite ammo, meaning it's usually going to be your first choice when killing the baddies. There's also a shotgun, which can kill baddies in 2-4 shots depending on their strength and distance, an automatic shotgun, which is very rare, and I believe only found in later levels, a rocket launcher, which can select either homing missiles or regular missiles, some kind of fire launcher that fires a projectile that sets fire for a short distance in front of you, and then there's the classic flamethrower that burns everyone to a crisp, leaving them running as they do so. 

You also have molotovs, which explode into a firey blaze that sends victims running and burning, grenades, which cause a small explosion and 3 different landmines, one of which is timed, one that will do a small fatal explosion, and one that does a large explosion for less damage.

Recently, they've added an update that adds more modern controls, but you can still use the classic controls in the options. Instead of having the mouse cursor locked in front of you, this update allows the user to point and click in a similar way to Hatred and Postal redux. I like it, and I feel like it allows the Postal Dude to be more mobile, especially when you're circling around an enemy shooting them with the machine gun.

I'd also like to thank Rich for informing me about this update, but I want to apologize for not taking the time to play it until today.

Revisiting yet another game I merely glossed over as a dumb kid. I was awfully hostile for this game despite barely giving it a chance, and also in spite of me absolutely loving it's sequel, Postal 2. These games are diametrically opposed to one another in gameplay and objective. Both are crude, offensive, but where they're really complimenting each other, and where their sequels fail, is in how Postal 1 and 2 explore brutal violence, and how in the format of the medium, these presentations can produce vastly different results.

Postal 1 is a harsh and oppressive experience. It's objective, in contrast to it's sequel, is to kill everything in sight with a small variety of weapons. You have an M18, A shotgun and machine gun which, for whatever reason share ammunition as an interesting way to balance difficulty, a rocket launcher with 2 types of ammunition, grenades, molotovs, a napalm launcher, a flamethrower, and a variety of landmines which I found completely superfluous, and you control the dude from a detached, omniscient third person perspective across a variety of linear stages. Some enemies are hostile, some civilians are completely innocent. I got an achievement for beating the game after killing every single one of them. It's honestly pretty basic.

However by it's end, you're confronted with the elementary school scene, followed by graphic depictions of the dude being locked up in an insane asylum with some of the most grating and harsh audio I've heard in a videogame - and after it's done it's clear that the game isn't exactly fun. Cathartic, sure, but not fun in the traditional sense of, a zillion other games that exist. Playing Postal 1 is a repetitive, janky experience with some oddball crude humour placed here and there. But in between, the game can be vastly dull, detached from any emotional experience.

Stumbling upon various pockets of the map can yeild rewards like extra health, armour or ammunition. It also sometimes might clue you in onto the experiential consciousness of a psychopathic mass murderer, with various audio cues of a kind of inner-ear drone, a low register tinnitus I guess. The sound design here is so deliberate in it's craft. When you're busy blasting away at these NPCs, they can all collectively scream, wail, into this cacophanous wall of noise. It's moments like these that can make the gamer speculate on what kind of scenario this is. In a way, Postal 1 reminded me of Elephant (2003) by Gus Van Sant, which incorporates a similar element of audio design, and Angst (1983) for it's detached, omniscient camera. There's this unspeakable horror on display, and these moments are the key strengths to Postal 1's presentation.

But, it's postal. In it's crassness, the game offers silly, crude moments that disperse it - one of those audio cues is a howling monkey. Another is a portable toilet that you can hear farts come out of. In a way, I think that, the commentary is that the game devs are showing a juvenile side to senseless violence - but it takes away from that oppression. It's not nearly as confronting as an experience as a result. I think it's a weakness to the games overall tone, one devoid of absolutely every single shred of humanity. A big part of why I didn't enjoy the game back when I originally played it as a kid is that, you don't have the option to play as a pacifist. It simultaneously missed the point, but rings true as to Postal 1 being an unenjoyable experience.

The Developers set out to achieve something graphic, violent, and extreme, and as a result, Postal 1 is shockingly boundary pushing as interactive art. Considering the state of politics and video games in 1994, the game was so taboo that it was a figure in radical art and the demand for censorship towards interactive media. We now know that games don't cause violence - there are several things that cause violence in people - social isolation, warped ideologies, extreme conditions of living, whatever. The point isn't determining a reason. It could merely be an overwhelming anger, complete unreason, and this is something that the Postal games nail down on - it is senseless violence in which you are a participant, you are completely restricted into performing violence in a cyclical, and repetitive fashion, and it's so effective in disturbing and especially, confronting.

A big part of why I never played the game as a kid and didn't really give it a chance as a kid, was that, it was scary. Postal opens with an instantaneous, visious wall of noise, and psychotically cobbled visuals where you can distinguish a screaming mouth, a man surrounded by skulls, and the loading screens hardly get more comforting. In that, there is a dread, a horror, that scared me off - and fighting past that discomfort, now numb as an adult, I think, is demonstrating a desensitisation to violence... or at least, oppressive tones and styles in media.

Real violence is completely different to what's depicted in Postal 1 and 2. You can see a dead body on the internet, but it isn't the same as seeing a dead body in real life, and that's because computers allow us to be voyeurs of discomforting material in comfortable environments. But they're as close to honest explorations of what violence is, and what extreme and graphic content can do to our psyches and minds. Psychopathy and violence when found in real life is something so much more primal, and cruel. At the time of Postal 1, the ending is something the developers thought was so absurd, bizarre, cruel that they didn't think it possible. But since columbine, and several hundreds of more mass shooting occuring in schools, it has since become a grisly, depressing reality. To be in a situation as violent as that must be scary for anyone. 

To murder is to take the matter of extinguishing a consciousness from a living being irreversibly, to think, and feel and touch, taken away. Postal 1 offers none of that.
